paper_title: ECHO: Efficient Causal Self-Recursion Beyond Auxiliary Multi-Token Prediction

sections.title: Abstract
sections.content: Existing Multi-token prediction (MTP) methods are auxiliary by design: the multi-horizon loss mostly trains modules attached to the backbone, and each added horizon costs another module and another pass. We propose Efficient Causal Self-Recursion (ECHO), which removes both costs. The backbone's own final layer predicts every horizon, so the supervision lands on the parameters that generate the next token, and Dynamic Depth Sampling (DDS) keeps deeper horizons affordable by drawing the training depth with probabilities that decay along depth. Future prediction thus becomes part of the autoregressive objective rather than a task attached to it, and the gains follow on both sides of it. In pretraining, added depth converts into downstream accuracy where auxiliary modules saturate, concentrating on reasoning and code at half the MTP training overhead of training every depth. At inference, the pretrained model is its own drafter: it drafts beyond the depth it was trained for, and keeps its draft-target alignment on the open-ended, high-entropy generation where post-hoc drafters lose theirs. The advantage survives a doubled token budget, a repeated pretraining run, and supervised finetuning.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content: Large language models (LLMs) (Achiam et al., 2023; Touvron et al., 2023; Bai et al., 2023; Liu et al., 2024a) are predominantly trained with the Next-Token Prediction (NTP) objective. While NTP has demonstrated remarkable scalability and effectiveness, it provides supervision only at the immediate next-token horizon, leaving potentially useful future information unexploited. Moreover, autoregressive decoding remains inherently sequential, resulting in limited inference throughput. To better utilize future information, recent work has explored Multi-Token Prediction (MTP) as an auxiliary objective on top of NTP. By introducing additional future-token prediction targets, MTP provides denser supervision during training and can generate draft tokens for speculative decoding, enabling inference acceleration. Early MTP methods predict multiple future positions independently from the same hidden state Gloeckle et al. (2024), providing denser supervision but ignoring causal dependencies among future tokens. Subsequent causal MTP methods such as DeepSeek-V3 Liu et al. (2024a) address this limitation by introducing autoregressive dependencies among future prediction steps, significantly improving prediction quality and improving the backbone models overall performance Liu et al. (2024a); Blakeman et al. (2025); Zeng et al. (2026). However, both causal and parallel MTP remain auxiliary by construction: future-token prediction is carried out by dedicated modules attached to the backbone, rather than being integrated into the autoregressive generation process itself. This leads to two limitations: 1. Indirect Multi-Horizon Supervision MTP losses primarily supervise the auxiliary prediction modules. Consequently, the backbone model receives multi-horizon learning signals only indirectly, potentially limiting their impact on long-horizon planning. 2. Costly Long-Horizon Supervision Denser supervision requires deeper prediction horizons, yet each additional horizon adds prediction module in memory and another pass in compute. This cost limits the prediction horizon in large-scale causal MTP pretraining, typically to single draft token. To address the above limitations, we introduce Efficient Causal Self-Recursion (ECHO), causal selfrecursive framework that reuses the backbones final layer for future prediction and samples per-step prediction depths with decaying probabilities to reduce the amortized MTP training overhead. Final-layer parameter sharing ensures that multi-horizon losses directly shape the backbone, rather than being absorbed by horizon-specific auxiliary modules. As shown in Figure 3a, this allows ECHO to benefit from deeper supervision: its downstream performance continues to improve at depth 3, whereas DeepSeeks MTP (Liu et al., 2024a) does not, consistent with observations in MiMo (LLM-Core Xiaomi, 2025). More fundamentally, training the same parameters responsible for next-token generation to predict multiple future tokens encourages the backbone to anticipate how the sequence unfolds over subsequent steps, as evidenced by ECHOs substantial gains on reasoning tasks. To make long-horizon supervision computationally efficient, we introduce Dynamic Depth Sampling (DDS), which samples prediction depths with decaying probabilities. This simultaneously reduces the amortized MTP training overhead and mitigates the impact of increasing prediction errors and supervision noise at greater depths. After supervised finetuning, ECHOs advantage grows further. Beyond its pretraining benefits, ECHO entirely eliminates the need for post-hoc drafter finetuning. DDS makes longer-horizon supervision affordable, while final-layer parameter sharing enables depth extrapolation: since the same shared layer is reused at every draft step, ECHO can extend drafting beyond the trained prediction depth while maintaining high acceptance rates, at an amortized MTP training overhead of only 1.5 depth-1 steps (see Section 4.1). By drafting directly with its pretrained weights, ECHO avoids the overfitting to academic benchmarks associated with post-hoc drafter finetuning (Liu et al., 2026), yielding substantial acceptance-length gains in realistic, high-entropy generation settings as shown in Figure 3b. Our main contributions are summarized as follows: We introduce Efficient Causal Self-Recursion (ECHO), which predicts every future horizon by recursively applying the backbones own final layer, with the per-step prediction depth drawn from distribution decaying along depth. ECHO-1.5(3) matches ECHO-3s gain at half its MTP overhead. (b) Accepted length against serving depth K, filled inside the trained depth and hollow beyond it. ECHO keeps gaining where auxiliary MTP saturates. ECHO makes long-horizon prediction cheap in compute and free in parameters, and keeps gaining acceptance when extrapolating in depth, where auxiliary MTP saturates. It eliminates drafter finetuning entirely, yet outperforms post-hoc drafters, especially on open-ended generation.

sections.title: 2 Related Work
sections.content: 2.1 Multi-Token Prediction Multi-Token Prediction (MTP) augments next-token prediction with future-token targets, improving language modeling while providing draft tokens for speculative decoding. It inherits the architecture of speculative draft models and differs in the training regime: draft models are finetuned post-hoc against frozen backbone on limited dataset, whereas MTP modules are optimized jointly with the backbone throughout pretraining. Parallel MTP predicts multiple future positions independently from several output heads on shared backbone Gloeckle et al. (2024), following Medusa Cai et al. (2024). Causal MTP instead follows EAGLE Li et al. (2024): DeepSeek-V3 Liu et al. (2024a) feeds dedicated prediction modules the previous hidden state together with shifted token embeddings, preserving autoregressive dependencies among future steps, and GLM-5 Zeng et al. (2026) shares those parameters across all depths, as EAGLE does, to reduce memory cost. 2.2 Post-hoc Drafter Post-hoc drafters are trained on top of frozen target model by finetuning on target-generated responses, and differ mainly in how block of draft tokens is produced. Medusa Cai et al. (2024) attaches parallel heads that draft every position from the final hidden state, while EAGLE-3 Li et al. (2025) re-enters lightweight decoder once per drafted token, conditioned on target hidden states, preserving tokento-token dependency. Recent parallel drafters build on DFlash Chen et al. (2026), which predicts the whole block in one pass, with DSpark Cheng et al. (2026) restoring intra-block dependency through lightweight causal head. Two limitations are nonetheless inherent to post-hoc drafting. First, the drafter is narrowly aligned with the target, being finetuned on dataset orders of magnitude smaller than the pretraining corpus. ECHO overcomes both: joint pretraining aligns it with the target, and its supervision improves the backbone at modest overhead. 2.3 Looped Transformers Looped transformers reuse shared block of layers across iterations, buying computational depth without new parameters: parameter efficiency (Lan et al., 2020), adaptive computation (Dehghani et al., 2019), reasoning at LLM scale (Saunshi et al., 2025; Zhu et al., 2025), test-time compute scaling (Geiping et al., 2025), and depth allocated per token (Bae et al., 2025). In all of them recursion refines the same token position under next-token objective; ECHO instead recurses along the horizon, each step conditioning on the next future token to predict one position further ahead. Yet both buy structure rather than recall, and for looping that is trade: at matched parameters and compute it leads on reasoning but trails on perplexity and closed-book QA (Saunshi et al., 2025), and at scale its gain is credited to knowledge manipulation rather than capacity, measured against external dense families rather than same-recipe baseline (Zhu et al., 2025). ECHO pays no such price: mathematics, reasoning and code gain while multiple choice and closed-book QA hold (Figure 3a), and both classes gain after finetuning (Figure 4b). Looping, latent chain-of-thought (Hao et al., 2025) and ECHO thus price latent computation differently: repeated passes over one position, annotated chains, and extra positions the one price that accepted tokens can repay.

sections.title: 3 ECHO: Efficient Causal Self-Recursion
sections.content: We first show that final-layer sharing benefits the backbone through direct multi-horizon supervision, and then dynamic depth sampling makes it affordable at greater depth. 3.1 Direct Multi-Horizon Supervision via Final-Layer Sharing We show that reusing the backbones final layer turns multi-horizon supervision into direct training signal: downstream performance improves over auxiliary MTP, and shows further gains at greater depth. Causal Self-Recursion: we follow the autoregressive design of DeepSeek-V3 (Liu et al., 2024a) to preserve causal dependency, where each additional horizon is predicted from the previous final-layer hidden state hL t1 and the embedding e(yt) of the previously predicted token. We show two benefits of the resulting direct multi-horizon supervision: Sharing improves downstream performance, especially in reasoning capability. To isolate the effect of sharing, we compare ECHO with DeepSeeks MTP (Liu et al., 2024a) at matched prediction depth (Figure 3a). Under this comparison, sharing the final layer gives ECHO the lead at depth 1, most clearly on math, reasoning and code (+0.79, +0.57 and +1.35), and it reaches +2.63 on reasoning and +2.23 on code at depth 3. The difference lies in where multi-horizon supervision mainly lands. With auxiliary modules, the signal is largely absorbed by the modules dedicated to individual horizons, leaving the backbones hidden layers specialized for the next token (Mehra et al., 2025). Sharing removes this bottleneck by construction: since the final layer predicts every horizon, supervision from all horizons is concentrated on the parameters that generate the next token. Sharing promotes longer-horizon supervision. To examine how each design uses added depth, we compare each family with itself from depth 1 to depth 3. Averaged over all fourteen benchmarks, deeper supervision improves ECHO by 0.63 points, whereas DeepSeeks MTP gains only 0.16, and ECHOs advantage on reasoning and code persists as depth increases (Figure 3a). This divergence follows from where each new horizons loss goes: in ECHO it reaches the backbone directly, whereas in DeepSeeks MTP it mostly trains the newly added module, as discussed above. This explains why auxiliary MTP rarely goes deeper in practice: DeepSeek-V3 trains with single MTP module (Liu et al., 2024a), and MiMo finds that adding MTP layers brings no further improvement (LLM-Core Xiaomi, 2025). 3.2 Affordable Long-Horizon Supervision via Dynamic Depth Sampling (DDS) We show that dynamically sampling the training depth lowers the cost of long-horizon supervision without sacrificing its gains in downstream performance and drafting quality. At this cost, ECHO-1.5(3) also outperforms MTP-1 on math, reasoning and code (+1.00, +1.31, +2.37) and still leads MTP-3 at twice its budget (+0.55, +2.31, +1.67; Figure 3a and Table 1).

The reasoning & code advantage therefore survives both conditions and the run-to-run spread, while the QA & multiple choice difference stays inside it. 4.2 Staying Aligned under realistic setting We then show that ECHO outperforms existing post-hoc drafters, with larger gains on high-entropy, realistic, and open-ended tasks, thanks to two complementary factors: causal drafting ensures consistency among draft tokens, while joint pretraining aligns the draft distribution with the target. Causal Drafting Matters in Open-Ended Generation. As shown in Figure 3b, ECHO and other causal drafters outperform parallel drafters on high-entropy tasks, consistent with Liu et al. (2026); Figure 8 shows the same ordering in decode speedup. When the next tokens are uncertain, the targets choice is hard to anticipate, so the probability of acceptance falls off steeply with depth and most of long draft is discarded. causal drafter adapts to this by extending its draft step by step, while parallel drafter emits fixed-length block whose deeper tokens are mostly rejected at verification. The balance shifts on simple code and mathematics benchmarks such as HumanEval, MBPP, and GSM8K, where long stretches of output are determined by syntax or derivation, and block-parallel drafting becomes worthwhile (Liu et al., 2026), whereas realistic software engineering tasks such as SWE-bench remain high-entropy and still favor causal drafting (Figure 3b). Such simple tasks, however, are small fraction of real-world usage, account for under 8% of consumer ChatGPT messages, while open-ended practical guidance, information seeking, and writing account for nearly 80% (Chatterji et al., 2025). Joint Pretraining Closes the Alignment Gap. Acceptance depends on how closely the draft distribution matches the targets (Leviathan et al., 2023; Zhou et al., 2024), and drafter can better match the target where it has seen the targets data. ECHO is trained with the target end-to-end and sees its full pretraining corpus. In contrast, auxiliary drafters are fit to frozen target on small finetuning set, so their acceptance drops under distribution shift (Liu et al., 2024b; Hong et al., 2025). The EAGLE-3 pair in Figure 3b isolates this effect: with architecture and finetuning data held fixed, warm-started EAGLE-3 achieves longer accepted length than its cold-start counterpart, consistent with recent findings that pretrained initialization strengthens drafters, most on out-of-domain inputs (Bie et al., 2026). Yet on open-ended tasks, warm-starting still falls short of ECHO, with the largest gap on SWE-bench. ECHO is instead optimized jointly with the target on every pretraining update, so its alignment is maintained throughout training, in line with the high acceptance rates reported for MTP modules trained jointly during pretraining (Liu et al., 2024a; LLM-Core Xiaomi, 2025).

sections.title: 5 The Advantage Holds across Data, Depth and Runs
sections.content: We finally examine whether ECHOs advantage holds along three axes: more pretraining data, deeper sampling, and repeated runs. 7 ECHO: Efficient Causal Self-Recursion Oct 17, 2026 5.1 Scaling with Data ECHOs advantage persists with more pretraining data. We extend pretraining of ECHO-1 and DeepSeeks MTP-1 from step 78k to step 156k, doubling the token budget. Both models improve, and ECHO-1 keeps its lead over DeepSeeks MTP-1 measured at the same step: +0.52 at step 78k and +0.50 at step 156k, and on reasoning & code it is +0.88 and +0.89 (Figure 4c, Table 2). This indicates that ECHOs advantage is stable under data scaling rather than an early-training effect that more data would erase. 5.2 Scaling with Depth ECHOs advantage holds across sampling depths. We next train ECHO-2(7), which samples over {1, . . . , 7} with E[D] = 2, at 4/3 the MTP training overhead of ECHO-1.5(3). It trails ECHO-1.5(3) in pretraining but overtakes it after SFT by 0.49, reaching the largest lead over DeepSeeks MTP-Instruct of any configuration (+2.10; Table 3). The gap in pretraining may be due to errors accumulating at deeper positions, which makes their supervision noisier and draws training away from the reliable shallow depths. After SFT, however, the deeper supervision appears to pay off, possibly because finetuning makes better use of what the backbone learned. 5.3 Stability across Runs ECHOs lead is robust to training and evaluation noise. reported gap can come from noise rather than the method itself. We eliminate evaluation noise by decoding greedily, so the remaining source is training. To measure it, we pretrain ECHO-1 and DeepSeeks MTP-1 second time under the same recipe and compare the two runs at the same step. Across the two runs, ECHO leads DeepSeeks MTP-1 by +0.52 and +0.78, and its lead on reasoning & code shifts by only 0.11 (Figure 4c; Section D). ECHOs overall and reasoning & code leads are therefore reproducible across runs.

sections.title: 6 Experiment Setup
sections.content: Full architecture, prompt, scoring and speculative decoding details are given in Section A. Models and Baselines: Every configuration shares 10B-A1B Latent MoE backbone (Blakeman et al., 2025) with 24 layers, multi-head latent attention (Liu et al., 2024a), and 256 routed experts with eight active per token (Dai et al., 2024), trained under the same recipe so that the comparison isolates the MTP design. Pretraining: 600B tokens at sequence length 4,096 and batch size 1,920 in bfloat16 with Muon (Jordan et al., 2024), on 24 nodes of eight H800 GPUs. Dynamic Depth Sampling: ECHO-1.5(3) samples over {1, 2, 3} with π = (0.6, 0.3, 0.1), giving E[D] = 1.5 and ECHO-2(7) samples over {1, . . . , 7} with π = (0.520, 0.220, 0.121, 0.068, 0.036, 0.019, 0.016), giving E[D] = 2. Supervised Finetuning: Every configuration is finetuned with the same recipe, 5,000 steps over one pass of an in-house chat corpus at context length 32,768, keeping its pretrained MTP depths. Computational Cost: Each pretraining run takes approximately 3 days on 192 NVIDIA H800 GPUs with global batch size of 1,920, followed by 5 hours of SFT on the same hardware. Post-hoc drafter training uses 24 H800 GPUs with global batch size of 48, requiring about 22 hours for EAGLE-3, 19 hours for DFlash, and 55 hours for DSpark. Benchmark Evaluation: Fourteen few-shot (Brown et al., 2020) benchmarks decoded greedily, grouped by task form into mathematics, reasoning, multi-subject multiple choice, code and closed-book question answering, with CoT prompting (Wei et al., 2022) on MATH, GSM8K and BBH. Speculative decoding: We adopt the same temperature setting (T = 1) for both the target and draft models, following Bebop (Li et al., 2026b) and GLM-5.2 (GLM Team, 2026). This matters for RL training: rejection sampling with draft temperature> 0 keeps acceptance stable as target entropy rises, whereas greedy drafting degrades sharply at higher temperatures (Li et al., 2026b). All drafters are served with SGLang on single node of eight H800 GPUs and budget-matched at seven proposed positions plus one bonus token per verification step. We report decode-only throughput and mean accepted length on ten tasks, split by the target models predictive entropy into predictable and open-ended groups. 8 ECHO: Efficient Causal Self-Recursion Oct 17,

sections.title: 7 Conclusion
sections.content: We presented ECHO, which turns multi-token prediction from an auxiliary task into part of the autoregressive objective. By reusing the backbones own final layer at every horizon, ECHO lets multi-horizon supervision shape the parameters that generate the next token, and Dynamic Depth Sampling makes deeper horizons affordable by training them less often. Unlike auxiliary MTP such as DeepSeek, ECHO improves with added depth, and ECHO-1.5(3) matches the downstream gain of ECHO-3 at half the MTP overhead. At inference, the same shared layer makes the pretrained model its own drafter with close draft-target alignment: it drafts beyond its trained depth where auxiliary modules saturate, and it outperforms post-hoc drafters on open-ended, high-entropy generation. This advantage holds under doubled token budget, repeated pretraining run, and supervised finetuning.

sections.title: Limitations
sections.content: Due to compute constraints, pretraining was repeated once and finetuning was run with single seed. How far the gains from added depth and from depth extrapolation extend, how DDS behaves at greater depths, and why deeper sampling pays off only after finetuning are left to future work. 9 ECHO: Efficient Causal Self-Recursion Oct 17,

sections.title: A Experiment Setup
sections.content: A.1 Pretraining Model Architecture: The backbone is 10B-A1B Latent Mixture-of-Experts transformer (Blakeman et al., 2025), that is 10B parameters in total with 1B activated per token, stacked as 24 layers of hidden size 1,024 with 16 attention heads. Attention is multi-head latent (Liu et al., 2024a), with 512-dimensional query and keyvalue latents, and we add gated attention (Qiu et al., 2025), per-head querykey normalization and rotary positional embeddings (Su et al., 2024). Every layer is mixture of experts in latent space: the expert block projects the hidden state down to 512 dimensions, runs 256 fine-grained routed experts (Dai et al., 2024) of intermediate size 1,024 there, and projects back, with the router reading the hidden state rather than the latent. sigmoid gate sends each token to eight routed experts, balanced by sequence-level auxiliary loss, plus one shared expert. The SwiGLU (Shazeer, 2020) feed-forward width is 5,120 and the vocabulary holds 201,216 tokens. Training Settings: We train the model on 600B tokens with context sequence length of 4,096 and global batch size of 1,920. Training uses bfloat16 precision and the Muon optimizer (Jordan et al., 2024), with AdamW retained for the embeddings, the biases, the output head and the expert router, learning rate of 6 104, warmup of 1,000 steps, weight decay of 0.1, and gradient clipping at 1.0. Following Liu et al. (2024a), we set the MTP loss scaling factor to 0.3. Pretraining runs on 24 nodes of eight H800 GPUs each, with eight-way expert parallelism, stage-one optimizer sharding, no tensor or pipeline parallelism, and full activation recomputation. Computational Cost: Each pretraining run is conducted on 24 nodes with eight NVIDIA H800 80GB GPUs per node (192 GPUs in total), taking approximately three days to complete. Supervised finetuning uses the same hardware configuration and takes approximately five hours per run. For the post-hoc speculative decoding baselines, we train the draft models on three nodes (24 H800 80GB GPUs), using global batch size of 48. EAGLE-3 (cold-start and warm-start) and DFlash use per-GPU batch size of 2 without gradient accumulation, whereas DSpark uses per-GPU batch size of 1 with two gradient accumulation steps due to GPU memory constraints. EAGLE-3 requires approximately 22 hours per run in measured wall-clock time. Based on the recorded compute time and an estimated 1.27 overhead for startup, checkpointing, and cluster variability, DSpark requires approximately 55 hours, while DFlash requires approximately 19 hours. Methods Compared: All six configurations are trained under the recipe above, so the comparison isolates the MTP design. ECHO reuses the backbones last layer as the body of every MTP depth; DeepSeeks MTP baselines follow Liu et al. (2024a) and keep an independent module per depth, sharing only the embedding and the output head. ECHO-1 and MTP-1 train one depth, ECHO-3 and MTP-3 train three at every step, ECHO-1.5(3) samples depths one to three with E[D] = 1.5, and ECHO-2(7) extends dynamic depth sampling to depths one through seven with E[D] = 2. The two cost-matched comparisons are ECHO-1 against MTP-1 at equal depth-one cost, and ECHO-1.5(3) against MTP-3 at half the MTP cost. Dynamic Depth Sampling: The sampled depth is π, where π places probabilities 0.6, 0.3 and 0.1 on depths 1, 2 and 3, so E[D] = 1.5. Each optimizer step draws one and trains depths 1 through D, and every micro-batch in the step shares the same D, which keeps per-step compute constant. Averaging the loss over the trained depths gives depth the weight E[1{D d}/D], and these weights sum to one: ECHO reweights depths by how often it samples them, not by attaching per-depth loss coefficient. is deterministic function of the seed and the step index, so every rank derives it without communication and resumed run continues the same sequence. Supervised Finetuning: All configurations adopt an identical recipe: 5,000 steps over one pass of an in-house chat SFT corpus at context length of 32,768, with eight-way context parallelism. Each keeps the MTP depths it was pretrained with, so the finetuned comparison isolates the same design difference as the pretrained one. A.2 Benchmark Evaluation Evaluation Setup: We evaluate the pretrained checkpoints on fourteen few-shot benchmarks, grouped by the form of the task following Liu et al. (2024a): mathematics with MATH (Hendrycks et al., 2021b) and GSM8K (Cobbe et al., 2021); reasoning with BBH (Suzgun et al., 2023), BBEH (Kazemi et al., 2025), WinoGrande (Sakaguchi et al., 2021) and PIQA (Bisk et al., 2020); multi-subject multiple choice with MMLU (Hendrycks et al., 2021a) and MMLU-Pro (Wang et al., 2024); code with HumanEval+ and MBPP+ (Liu et al., 2023) and LiveCodeBench (Jain et al., 2025); closed-book question answering with PopQA (Mallen et al., 2023), PreciseWikiQA (Bang et al., 2025) and HotpotQA (Yang et al., 2018). We report unweighted averages within each group and across all fourteen benchmarks. Benchmarks such as GPQA 14 ECHO: Efficient Causal Self-Recursion Oct 17, 2026 (Rein et al., 2024), SimpleQA (Wei et al., 2024) and HMMT are left out for lack of resolution rather than for any defect in their scoring: every configuration scores near their floor, so the row moves more than it resolves. Prompts and Decoding: All benchmarks are evaluated in the few-shot in-context format (Brown et al., 2020). Chain-of-thought prompting (Wei et al., 2022) is used on MATH, GSM8K and BBH, with eight, eight and four demonstrations respectively. The remaining benchmarks are prompted to answer directly, with five demonstrations for the multiple-choice benchmarks, ten for closed-book question answering and two for BBEH. BBH is released under both chain-of-thought and an answer-directly prompt over the same items for examining the chain-of-thought effect (Suzgun et al., 2023); we report its chain-of-thought form in the main results. Decoding is greedy throughout. Generation is capped per benchmark: two tokens for MMLU and eleven for MMLU-Pro, which are answered with single option label; 65 for the closed-book sets and 101 for PopQA; 401 for MATH, 512 for GSM8K, BBEH and HumanEval+, 601 for BBH, 768 for LiveCodeBench and 8192 for MBPP+. WinoGrande and PIQA involve no generation. Stop sequences are applied when the answer is extracted rather than during decoding, so the cap is what bounds each output. Scoring and Averaging: Each benchmarks score is an unweighted macro-average over its sub-tasks rather than per-item micro-average. Four scoring rules are used, one per group of benchmarks. GSM8K, MATH, BBH, MMLU and MMLU-Pro are scored by rule from the extracted answer. HumanEval+, MBPP+ and LiveCodeBench are scored as pass@1 by execution (Chen et al., 2021). WinoGrande and PIQA are scored by length-normalized log-likelihood over the candidate continuations rather than by generation, as in Liu et al. (2024a), with the normalization of Gao et al. (2024). PreciseWikiQA, HotpotQA, PopQA and BBEH are graded against the reference answer by an LLM judge. In Table 1 the three factual-knowledge sets are graded by gpt-oss-120b and BBEH by Claude Opus 4.8; in Table 3 all four are graded by Claude Opus 4.8. Of these, the three factual-knowledge sets report the F1 of overall accuracy and accuracy among attempted items, with abstentions in the denominator of the former only. Category averages and the overall figure are unweighted means over benchmarks. A.3 Speculative Decoding under Serving Serving Stack: All serving measurements use SGLang on one node of eight H800 GPUs, with tensor parallelism 8 and FlashAttention-3. Drafters: All drafters are budget-matched at seven proposed positions plus one target bonus token, i.e. eight verification slots per request per step. ECHO reuses the targets final layer and full output head. EAGLE-3 (Li et al., 2025) uses one draft layer with reduced 32,000-entry head scattered back to target width, in cold-start and warm-start variant; following Kimi Team (2026), the warm start initializes the draft from DeepSeeks pretrained MTP weights, and is always normalized by the baseline of its own run. DSpark (Cheng et al., 2026) and DFlash (Chen et al., 2026) are block-parallel with five draft layers, the former adding low-rank Markov transition bias. Serving Metric: We report decode-only throughput, decoded tokens over summed per-request decode latency, which excludes prefill; metrics that include prefill confound the comparison across tasks with differing prompt lengths. Speedup is recomputed against the baseline of the same run, and accepted length is decoded tokens per verification step. Tasks: Serving results use ten tasks in two groups, split by predictive entropy as in Liu et al. (2026). Predictable, following the commonly adopted SpecForge benchmarks (Li et al., 2026a): HumanEval, MBPP, MATH-500, GSM8K, LiveCodeBench. Open-ended: SWE-bench, Arena-Hard, MT-Bench, summarization, Alpaca. Question answering, retrieval-augmented generation, translation and AIME-25 are excluded, all having median outputs of twenty to thirty tokens, too few verification steps for stable decode-only ratio. The entropy axis is the targets own predictive entropy, measured separately. Verification Budget: DSpark is evaluated with its confidence scheduler disabled, verifying the full draft block at every step, as in the diagnostic baseline of Cheng et al. (2026). The scheduler is calibrated cost model rather than threshold: it needs latency curve re-profiled for each GPU and backend (Cheng et al., 2026; Liu et al., 2026), and confidence head calibrated on the serving distribution, since the survival probabilities it multiplies must be absolute rather than merely well-ranked. That calibration does not transfer, because the mechanism assumes acceptance varies sharply across domains in the first place. With the head enabled but neither artifact available, per-step cost rose 514% and nothing was pruned. Depth Extrapolation: The depth sweep of Figure 1b uses separate harness. We report the accepted length obtained at serving depth K, τK = 1 + jK ij pi, for conditional acceptance rate pi at depth i. The expression is exact rather than fit: the draft loop reaches depth + 1 only after depth is accepted, so 15 ECHO: Efficient Causal Self-Recursion Oct 17, ij pi is the probability that the first drafted tokens are all accepted, and summing those probabilities gives their expected number. Runs use draft depth K=7, greedy on both sides, 256 new tokens, and pool GSM8K, HumanEval and MATH-500 weighted by rounds.

sections.title: D Stability across Pretraining Runs
sections.content: Two of the configurations were pretrained second time under the same recipe, and the comparison survives it. Over the fourteen benchmarks of the reported scope, ECHO MTP-1 leads DeepSeeks MTP-1 by 0.52 points in the baseline run and by 0.78 in the repeat. Two evaluations of the same weights differ by 0.27 points per benchmark, which puts the noise at 0.13 on fourteen-benchmark gap and 0.30 on category gap. Next-Token Loss Does Not Separate the Two Objectives Figure 5 separates the objective into its two terms. On the backbones next-token loss the two runs are indistinguishable: the gap averages 0.004 over the 78k steps and stays between 0.004 and 0.005 in every 10k-step window, with ECHO-1 marginally above MTP-1 throughout. The MTP loss carries larger gap in the same direction, 0.011 at step 78k. On the same token budget the two objectives therefore arrive at the same next-token likelihood, and neither margin is one the method is meant to win. Figure 5: Training loss of ECHO-1 and MTP-1 over the first 78k steps of the baseline run, separated into the backbones next-token loss (left) and the MTP loss (right). The logged objective is the weighted sum = Lbackbone + 0.3 LMTP, and the left panel is recovered by subtracting the weighted MTP loss from it. Each curve is an exponential moving average over all 78,000 logged steps, with no subsampling; the vertical range is clipped to what the curves occupy after step 12k, so the first few thousand steps run above the frame. This is the expected outcome rather than negative result. ECHOs multi-horizon objective adds no capacity to the next-token head; it changes what the shared representation is required to support. In predicting the next token the model is held responsible for several future positions at once, which constrains the hidden state towards features that stay predictive beyond one step. The effect of such constraint is regularization, and regularization does not surface in the quantity it constrains: next-token cross-entropy is the term both objectives already optimize, so matching it is the premise of the comparison rather than its outcome. The two configurations separate downstream instead, in the benchmark gaps of 18 ECHO: Efficient Causal Self-Recursion Oct 17, 2026 Tables 1 and 2 and in the draft quality that Section 4 converts into decode speedup. On the backbone term (left) the five lie within 0.006 and the ordering follows the family rather than the depth; the depth-1 term (right) is where added depth shows up. The same holds along depth. Figure 6 repeats the split for all five configurations, ECHO-1, ECHO-1.5(3) and ECHO-3 against MTP-1 and MTP-3, over the steps all the runs share. Within family the backbone term barely moves with depth: the three ECHO configurations end within 0.002 of each other, and MTP-3 sits 0.0017 below MTP-1. Across all five it spans 0.006, and the ordering is not ours to like MTP-3 holds the lowest backbone loss of any configuration, 1.676 against ECHO-3s 1.682, while ECHO-3 leads it by 0.97 points over the fourteen benchmarks of Table 1. What does move is the MTP term, and it moves the way the weighting predicts: the per-step loss is averaged over the depths trained at that step, so adding depths takes weight off depth 1, and the depth-1 term rises by 0.027 from ECHO-1.5(3) to ECHO-3 and by 0.048 from MTP-1 to MTP-3. At matched depth 3 the two designs divide the horizons: reusing the final layer fits the nearest one better (1.902 against 1.911) and the separate modules fit the far ones better (1.992 and 2.045 against 2.002 and 2.083 at depths 2 and 3). ECHO-1.5(3)s deeper terms are logged only on the steps that sample them, 39.5% and 9.8% of steps for depths 2 and 3, which is the fk = P(D k) = (1, 0.4, 0.1) that π = (0.6, 0.3, 0.1) prescribes in Equation (4). At matched step those sampled depths are where the saving is paid for: Figure 7 puts ECHO-1.5(3)s depth-2 term 0.051 above ECHO-3s at step 78k and its depth-3 term 0.132 above, with the curves running parallel rather than converging. That is the shape of the trade, and it stops there. Depth 1, which both train at every step, costs nothing at all (1.874 against 1.902, in ECHO-1.5(3)s favour); the fourteen-task average is within 0.02 (36.34 against 36.36, Table 1); and the accepted length holds beyond the trained depth (Figure 1b). None of these margins is where the comparison is settled, which is this sections point: the terms of the training objective do not rank the two designs.

sections.title: H Comparability of Reported Baselines in Inference
sections.content: The evaluation scales differ systematically. EAGLE-3 reports results across wide range of target sizes, from Vicuna-13B up to LLaMA-3.3-70B, whereas the parallel drafters cluster at the small end: Domino (Huang et al., 2026) evaluates only Qwen3-4B and Qwen3-8B, DSpark extends to Qwen3-14B, and the largest target any of them reports is Qwen3-Coder-30B-A3B, sparse model with roughly 3B active parameters, so its per-token cost is closer to 4B dense model than to 30B one.
